claim: The emergence of life on Earth dates back approximately 3.7–4.5 billion years.
source: It is estimated that this event dates back approximately 3.7–4.5 billion years, with fossil carbon isotope signatures being the oldest evidence for life around 3.7 billion years ago (Pearce et al., 2018; Rosing, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearce et al., 2018 and Rosing, 1999

claim: Fossil carbon isotope signatures are the oldest evidence for life around 3.7 billion years ago.
source: It is estimated that this event dates back approximately 3.7–4.5 billion years, with fossil carbon isotope signatures being the oldest evidence for life around 3.7 billion years ago (Pearce et al., 2018; Rosing, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearce et al., 2018 and Rosing, 1999

claim: Darwinian evolution of informational polymers was at the core of the origin of life.
source: The common theory is that the Darwinian evolution of informational polymers was at the core of the origin of life (Orgel, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Orgel, 1994

claim: Nucleic acids like RNA can both store genetic information and catalyze their own replication through transient formation of double-stranded helices.
source: Among these, nucleic acids, like RNA, stand out for their capability to both store genetic information and catalyze their own replication through transient formation of double-stranded helices (Gilbert, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilbert, 1986

claim: Prebiotic reactions require sufficiently high concentrations of their reagents to work.
source: Dilution, however, poses a significant obstacle, since such prebiotic reactions require sufficiently high concentrations of their reagents to work (Luisi, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luisi, 2015

claim: Large reservoirs such as the ocean cannot compensate for diffusion because they lack local sources of energy to drive reaction pathways out of equilibrium.
source: Large reservoirs, such as the ocean, cannot compensate for diffusion, because they lack local sources of energy to drive reaction pathways out of equilibrium (Goldenfeld and Woese, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldenfeld and Woese, 2011

claim: The homogeneity of large reservoirs renders these environments unlikely to have harbored early molecular life.
source: The resulting homogeneity renders these environments unlikely to have harbored early molecular life (Lane et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lane et al., 2010

claim: Local physical non-equilibria have shown the ability to up-concentrate molecules such as nucleic acids in a variety of different geological settings.
source: Local physical non-equilibria, however, have shown the ability to up-concentrate molecules, such as nucleic acids, in a variety of different geological settings (Ianeselli et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ianeselli et al., 2023

claim: Examples of geological settings that can up-concentrate molecules include thermal gradients in rock pores, local evaporation, re-hydration cycles of warm ponds, adsorption to mineral surfaces, heated gas bubbles in porous rocks, foams, and the eutectic phase in freeze-thaw cycles.
source: Examples range from thermal gradients in rock pores, local evaporation, re-hydration cycles of warm ponds, adsorption to mineral surfaces, heated gas bubbles in porous rocks, foams, or the eutectic phase in freeze-thaw cycles (Mast et al., 2013; Matreux et al., 2024; Pearce et al., 2017; Damer and Deamer, 2015; Ferris et al., 1996; Morasch et al., 2019; Tekin et al., 2022; Trinks et al., 2005; Stribling and Miller, 1991).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to various studies

claim: The melting temperature of oligonucleotides is strongly dependent on the local salt concentration.
source: But strand separation becomes increasingly difficult after accumulation, because the melting temperature of oligonucleotides is strongly dependent on the local salt concentration (Schildkraut and Lifson, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schildkraut and Lifson, 1965

claim: High Mg2+ concentrations are required for replication and catalytic activity.
source: Despite high Mg2+ concentrations being required for replication and catalytic activity (Hampel and Cowan, 1997), they can elevate the melting temperature of nucleic acid duplex structures to levels surpassing even the boiling point of water (Szostak, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hampel and Cowan, 1997

claim: High Mg2+ concentrations can elevate the melting temperature of nucleic acid duplex structures to levels surpassing even the boiling point of water.
source: Despite high Mg2+ concentrations being required for replication and catalytic activity (Hampel and Cowan, 1997), they can elevate the melting temperature of nucleic acid duplex structures to levels surpassing even the boiling point of water (Szostak, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Szostak, 2012

claim: Oligonucleotides readily hydrolyze into nucleotide fragments under high temperature conditions.
source: Oligonucleotides readily hydrolyze into nucleotide fragments under these conditions, rendering high temperature spikes as a primary strand separation mechanism more detrimental than beneficial (Li and Breaker, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Breaker, 1999

claim: pH oscillations can drive nucleic acid strand separation, caused either by differential thermophoresis of ionic species or by periodic freeze-thaw cycles.
source: Examples have used pH oscillations to drive nucleic acid strand separation, which can be caused either by differential thermophoresis of ionic species or by periodic freeze-thaw cycles (Mariani et al., 2018; Keil et al., 2017; Takenaka et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mariani et al., 2018; Keil et al., 2017; Takenaka et al., 2006

claim: Dew droplet cycles in a rock pore subjected to a temperature gradient can periodically melt strands by transiently lowering the salt concentration.
source: Also, dew droplet cycles in a rock pore subjected to a temperature gradient can periodically melt strands by transiently lowering the salt concentration (Ianeselli et al., 2019; Salditt et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ianeselli et al., 2019; Salditt et al., 2023

claim: Heated gas-water interfaces promote many prebiotic synthesis reactions.

evidence: Supported by citations to Deal et al., 2021; Morasch et al., 2019; Dass et al., 2023

claim: Gas-water evaporation interfaces can be found in the vicinity of underwater degassing events where gases percolate through rocks to reach the surface, or in porous rocks at the surface exposed to atmospheric winds.

claim: Volcanic islands on early Earth offered the necessary dry conditions for RNA synthesis.
